subsubtopic: SUGGESTION PRIME MINISTER BE REQUIRED TO DISCLOSE ALL DETAILS CONNECTED WITH CONSTRUCTION OF SWIMMING POOL-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to move a motion arising from the arrogant and incomplete answers given yesterday to questions on the order paper concerning the swimming pool constructed at the official residence of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) at 24 Sussex Drive, and also arising from the fact that this House has every right to find unacceptable continued evasion and misleading information on the matter. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie):
With specific reference to the answer of yesterday to question 1,233 which asked for numerous details concerning construction of and donors to the swimming pool at the Prime Minister's official residence at 24 Sussex Drive along with the answers to questions 1,684,1,686 and 1,687 on the same subject, it is the opinion of this House that the Prime Minister is withholding legitimate information from the elected representatives of the people, and that this constitutes not only an affront to parliament and the people of Canada, but also indicates the grave possibility that severe improprieties and conflict of interest factors most definitely do exist with regard to this matter: and finally, the House calls on the Prime Minister to forthwith make full disclosure and tell the entire truth to parliament.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask the unanimous consent of the House to introduce an important and urgent motion.
Since the costs of the 1976 Olympic Games, which were supposed to be moderate, have become astronomical if not disastrous and since the matter concerns and should concern all Canadians, especially at a time when the government is endeavouring to control inflation, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard):
That this House recommend that the government instruct the prices and incomes control commission to investigate the expenditures incurred up to now for the Montreal Olympic Games and to control other expenditures to be incurred till the games are held and even afterwards. In addition, that it recommend that the government take a direct part in financing the games through other new means.

REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH INNUIT OF QUEBEC FOR ONE MONTH-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. The Northern Quebec Innuit Association representing the Eskimos north of the 55th parallel in Quebec have been negotiating in good faith an agreement in principle signed on November 19, 1974, which is to be executed on November 1 of this week.
Despite satisfactory progress the Northern Quebec Innuit Association has requested that the negotiations be extended for one month to resolve outstanding differences. These negotiations are unique in that the Innuit in Canada for the first time are negotiating a way of life indigenous to northern Quebec for better than 4,000 years. This request for an additional month does not affect negotiations that have taken place to date nor affect developments occurring in northern Quebec, nor is it related to matters such as working conditions or hourly wages, but I must emphasize they are negotiating their future in Canada.
In view of the reasonable and responsible request to extend the negotiations for one month, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil):
That the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development who represents the government of Canada in these negotiations take immediate action to have the negotiations extended by one month.

he had such a contingency plan. subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-CONTINGENCY PLAN IN EVENT LABOUR FAILS TO COMPLY WITH PROGRAM

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-APPLICABILITY OF PRICE GUIDELINES TO FIRMS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA FOLLOWING REMOVAL OF PROVINCIAL FREEZE
ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-APPLICABILITY OF PRICE GUIDELINES TO FIRMS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA FOLLOWING REMOVAL OF PROVINCIAL FREEZE
speechtext:
Some of us might be excused for thinking it is a toss-up. Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Finance arising out of a statement by the Minister of Justice and quoted in yesterday's Vancouver Province. It seems to clearly indicate that that minister does not believe the government's price control policy will be effective. The Minister of Justice is quoted as saying that "the British Columbia government's price freeze on essential goods and services invites a sudden, wild increase in prices once the freeze is lifted January 1." Can the minister advise whether the federal government's price guidelines will apply to firms in British Columbia that are affected by the temporary price freeze, and whether he expects those guidelines to be effective in limiting price increases to those that may be required strictly on the basis of increased costs?

October 29, 1975
Oral Questions

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-APPLICABILITY OF PRICE GUIDELINES TO FIRMS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA FOLLOWING REMOVAL OF PROVINCIAL FREEZE

In that respect, it seems that the observations of the Minister of Justice, if fairly quoted by the hon. member, are indeed sound.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED PARTICIPATION OF ALL CANADIANS IN COST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the right hon. Prime Minister, I wish to put my question to the Acting Prime Minister.
Considering that the Olympic Games will cost roughly $1 billion and will probably end up with a deficit of several hundred million, could the Acting Prime Minister tell the House whether he intends to take measures so that the deficit incurred for the games will be shared by all Canadians, since all Canada is benefitting from the publicity and international prestige of the games?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED PARTICIPATION OF ALL CANADIANS IN COST

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR MEETING WITH NORTHERN QUEBEC INNUIT ASSOCIATION-POSSIBLE EXTENSION OF NEGOTIATIONS FOR ONE MONTH
speechtext: Such a request was made. I did not meet with them but I did discuss the situation with Charlie Watt, the President of the Northern Quebec Innuit Association at midnight last night. I am happy to report that they had a good day yesterday and indicated they had made substantial progress toward an agreement.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR MEETING WITH NORTHERN QUEBEC INNUIT ASSOCIATION-POSSIBLE EXTENSION OF NEGOTIATIONS FOR ONE MONTH
speechtext: I welcome the minister's comments. Has the hon. gentleman held additional discussions with the other parties involved in the negotiations with a view to extending the time frame for one month. subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR MEETING WITH NORTHERN QUEBEC INNUIT ASSOCIATION-POSSIBLE EXTENSION OF NEGOTIATIONS FOR ONE MONTH
speechtext: Basically we are not unsympathetic to the idea of extending the period, but the Grand Council of the Cree is absolutely opposed to any extension and is adamant that we sign the agreement on November 1. A procedure is being established in the agreement which is being negotiated which will provide for a period of 60 or 90 days during which a referendum would be held among the various communities to determine whether they are in favour of the agreement or against it.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR MEETING WITH NORTHERN QUEBEC INNUIT ASSOCIATION-POSSIBLE EXTENSION OF NEGOTIATIONS FOR ONE MONTH

In making this request I would point out that any precedent set here is likely to be followed for generations, and might possibly set a precedent for developments in the Northwest Territories also.

speechtext:
Oh, oh!

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the interest of hon. members opposite indicates that what I am speaking about has no relationship to their thinking. In view of the fact that the Prime Minister stated some years ago that ultimately the true facts would come out, since they have now done so over the CBC will parliament have the opportunity of discussing a matter which today has all the appearances of applied tyranny?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR DEBATE ON REASONS FOR INVOKING WAR MEASURES ACT IN OCTOBER, 1970-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I cannot accept necessarily the description that the right hon. gentleman has given of the action taken by our former colleague Mr. Kierans, but I would recommend that he read once again the letter that Premier Bourassa wrote to the Prime Minister which is to be found in Hansard for October, 1970. It sets out fully the reasons that the premier of Quebec, the mayor of Montreal and all those who had responsibility at that time made a very strong plea to the Canadian government to invoke the War Measures Act. They may have changed their minds now but at that time they were very clear. Perhaps one of the problems is that people do forget the circumstances at the time.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR DEBATE ON REASONS FOR INVOKING WAR MEASURES ACT IN OCTOBER, 1970-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. This is the first time there has been the revelation that the mayor of Montreal and the premier of Quebec determine the course of the people of Canada through the government. The minister still has not answered my question. In order to clarify the matter, not in the ex parte way the minister dealt with the question just now but in order to get the facts and to have Mr. Kierans and the premier of Quebec here, would the minister allow a date to be set aside so we can discuss the matter and determine the facts? Would he also tell the people of Canada whether the strategic operations centre that was described during that broadcast and which took over responsibility from the cabinet for what was called "crisis management"-a kind of CIA-is still in existence today?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, now that the Minister of Transport has had two or three days to catch up on the nomenclature of Maritime activities for which he is responsible, I would ask whether it is the intention of the government to close the Arctic exclusively for Canadian shipping in terms of the extractive resource industries there?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT INTENTIONS WITH REGARD TO USE OF CANADIAN SHIPS TO MOVE OIL FROM ARCTIC

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Transport and ask him if he would investigate the fact that CPR has been reducing its rolling stock by scrapping freight cars every day, many of them in good condition, a program which is contrary to the understanding which the minister had with the railways and which has led to the layoffs of almost 1,000 people in Winnipeg?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLEGED SCRAPPING OF FREIGHT CARS-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did some preliminary investigation when we purchased hopper cars. It was, of course, with the understanding contained in the subsequent agreement that the removal of regular cars could not be accelerated. It was never contemplated that all cars would be kept in service. I am told that so far as the CNR is concerned that agreement is being adhered to, and I believe it may also be true in relation to CPR, but we are looking further into that.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED SCRAPPING OF FREIGHT CARS-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION
speechtext: In view of the fact that there have been virtually no layoffs by the CNR but substantial layoffs in many cities in Canada by CPR, would the minister look into the question of whether CPR is in fact adhering to the agreement at which they arrived with the minister three years ago or whether CPR is exempt from following agreements and understandings which they made with the Government of Canada in good faith?

speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLEGED SCRAPPING OF FREIGHT CARS-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION
speechtext: Of course, they are not exempt, and I have indicated I have begun and will continue to look into that question. The layoff situation on the railways is in part due to the economic slow down in the economy and therefore a modification in the use of cars. When cars are used to a lesser extent, the repair required for those cars is also reduced. I think that explains some of the layoffs.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice. change in the criminal code. He is simply asking officers within his jurisdiction to enforce the law, and that would seem to be a good idea.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT

speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, October 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Andras that Bill C-69, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I called it ten o'clock last evening I was reminding the minister that during the speeches given by my colleagues, and especially during the speech given by the spokesman for our party on this issue, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), there were numerous very positive, reasonable and worth-while suggestions made as to how this legislation might be further improved. I suggested to the minister that he would be serving his own interests, the interests of the country and the interests of all Canadians if in fact during the course of the committee deliberations he were to look favourably on these suggestions which would improve the legislation even further.

October 29, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
These amendments are certainly necessary. It is agreed that the Unemployment Insurance Act as introduced in 1971 can only be described as a mess. It has cost the Canadian public many hundreds of millions of dollars, and improvement is long overdue. I am sure that no member of parliament or, for that matter, many Canadians, would seriously quarrel with the principle of unemployment insurance, that is, the principle that insurance should be provided to deal with the consequences of involuntary unemployment. However, I believe there has grown up amongst the Canadian people a vast amount of confusion and, indeed, resentment over vacillating government policies which on one hand give at one period of time, and on the other hand take away at another time.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in his Thanksgiving Day speech to the nation calling for severe restraint, stated:
All over the world, people are caught in the grip of what some have called the revolution of rising expectations. We have come to expect that there is some magic by which we can have cheap and plentiful food, energy, housing and government services, together with an ever improving standard of living. We expect this as a matter of right, regardless of how successful or unsuccessful we are in increasing our production of goods and services.
It is my opinion, and I am certain this feeling is shared by a great many citizens of Canada, that this Liberal government must take the major share of the responsibility for these rising expectations of the people of Canada. The Unemployment Insurance Act is only one example of Liberal government policies which have led the Canadian people to raise their expectations of government services to the point where the government is now calling for a program of restraint which, as the Prime Minister stated, is the heaviest imposed upon Canadians since the Second World War.
There are three measures in the proposed legislation which embody the principle of restraint. The first is an increase from three to six weeks in the period of disqualification for those who have quit, have been fired from their jobs or have refused suitable employment. I believe this provision is an improvement over the present legislation; it will undoubtedly reduce the number of abuses in respect of unemployment insurance benefits. The other two measures, termination of benefits at age 65 and the reduction of benefits to low income claimants, while contributing to restraint to some extent cannot, I feel, be justified on either economic or ethical grounds.
Let me expand on this point. Those in the labour force over age 65 have only a 10 per cent participation rate in the unemployment insurance scheme. Even if this entire group was receiving unemployment insurance benefits at the average Canadian rate of $74.61 per week for 15.9 weeks-and I emphasize that all these points are highly unlikely and have been overestimated-the total saving to the Government of Canada would be $2.77 million, or .07 per cent of this year's deficit. That is hardly significant, Mr. Speaker, in terms of employed persons over age 65. I believe the benefits to the government, whatever they may be, do not outweigh the detrimental effects felt by these persons. The provision to do away with the special benefit rate for low income claimants will affect those in dire circumstances, those to whom the benefits are most useful. In these three amendments we see measures which embody the principle of restraint. But can this restraint be

justified when it affects the poor and the aged, those least able to bear the added restraint?
When the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act were debated in committee in 1971, some opposition was expressed to the provision of retirement benefits since these were not seen as falling within the principle of unemployment insurance with respect to interruption of earnings. This opposition was brushed aside by the government, however, and the provision for retirement benefits was passed. I do not wish to seem unconcerned about the plight of our senior citizens; indeed, this concern has been expressed a great many times. But I wish to make the point that this is a concrete example of the government's contribution to the "revolution of rising expectations". The government puts the blame on the Canadian people for their rising expectations, while their policies contribute directly to this attitude: they give with one hand and take away with the other.
I have said that I approve of the provision to increase the disqualification period from three weeks to six weeks as I feel it is, taken over-all, a valid vehicle for restraint. Moreover, I feel it will contribute to shoring up the Unemployment Insurance Act in the badly needed area of work incentives. Indeed, this is the only amendment proposed for the Unemployment Insurance Act which is designed to deal with the problem of work incentives. The inclusion of work incentives goes back to the basic principle of unemployment insurance, one which has been debated many times over the past few years but which has become even more pressing as the cost of operating the Unemployment Insurance Act becomes more and more prohibitive. This principle concerns, of course, whether the payment of unemployment insurance benefits should be regarded as strictly insurance or whether it should include aspects of income supplement.
My colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton West, and others who have spoken in this debate have asked to what degree the Unemployment Insurance Act as presently constituted has undermined the work ethic in this country. The idea has been pooh-poohed by some, but not by those who have looked objectively at the effect on unemployment insurance. The destruction of the work ethic is something all Canadians should be concerned about. It represents a change in our society which is not an improvement.
Concern has been expressed about young people who show no concern for their future, about the degree of vandalism which is apparent, and about the disrespect for many features in our system. The statistics are alarming. I would not suggest that the Unemployment Insurance Commission is causing this, but I think it would be foolhardy not to recognize that the change in our sense of responsibility, in our appreciation of the importance of work, in the importance of initiative, and of being responsible each for his own welfare, has contributed to a general breakdown in our traditional patterns. If there is any improvement in conditions at all, it is an accident and is not due to the clear direction of this government.
The other aspect of the deterioration of the work ethic in this country is the drop in productivity of Canadian
October 29, 1975

labour. Recent statistics show that the drop has been dramatic in the last couple of years, and in fact is negative for the first time since figures have been recorded. The effects on our economy and our standard of living are extremely serious. It would be unfortunate if those in charge neglected the possibility that misconstrued and maladministered programs such as the UIC have contributed directly to that drop in productivity.
I would suggest that this government are taking an about-turn on the principle of unemployment insurance, not on the basis that they are concerned about the work ethic but, rather, on the grounds that the cost to the government is unwieldy and that the present act contains features which have undesirable effects on the work ethic. There is no question that the cost of the Unemployment Insurance program is becoming prohibitive. Benefit payments in 1974-75 amounted to $2.3 billion, with the government picking up $700 million. Benefit payments in 1975-76 are expected to exceed $3.75 billion, placing a total cost on the government of approximately $1.75 billion, an increase of 150 per cent over the previous year.
As to work incentives, while we support the extended disqualification period, the Progressive Conservative Party has proposed a measure which we feel would more directly contribute to fostering the incentive to work. We have suggested for some time that eligibility for unemployment insurance be based on an extended period in the work force. In the 1971 debate on amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act, we proposed that the eligibility period should be at least 12 weeks and not the eight weeks that is currently required. This extension would ensure that unemployment insurance would be directed to those who were securely tied to the work force, and as such it would be unemployment insurance and not just another welfare program open to public abuse. Such a measure would also contribute to restraint in a way that would be universal, and would not bear only on those least able to pay, as in the case of the aged and the poor.
I believe that the most valid criticism of the current proposals to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act can be made on the basis that the government openly courted rising expectations on the part of the Canadian people by opening the terms of reference of unemployment insurance benefits to include welfare payments as well as insurance against involuntary employment. Now that they have reaped the harvest of their policy, prohibitive costs and abuses due to work disincentive, they turn around and call for restraint on the part of the people of Canada. These restraints, however, would affect those least in a position to practice restraint.
In addition, the government has abdicated its responsibility for rising unemployment in Canada and the ensuing rising cost of unemployment insurance benefits. This has been accomplished by establishing a new unemployment benchmark, thereby ensuring that little or none of the additional cost of unemployment insurance will fall on the federal treasury in years ahead. Originally, the government arranged to lift the ceiling on its contribution to unemployment insurance benefits as the true cost of their 1971 amendments started rolling in and the ineffectiveness of their economic policies began to show up in unemployment figures, and now they have arranged to bury federal
Unemployment Insurance Act
government contributions by adding them as a direct tax on the Canadian people. It has been estimated that this new tax in the form of increased UIC payments will amount to $89 or more annually on the wages and salaries of Canadians.
If the government were really concerned about workers in Canadian society it would use all its expertise and experience to devise means for bringing more Canadians back into the work force. It would do this by utilizing all the resources of Manpower, by encouraging work and by incentives, and not, as can be seen in these amendments, merely by working out ways to finance unemployment insurance schemes at the expense of people who are low on the wage scale.
As justice must be seen to be done, and not merely done, so the government must devise amendments to the act which will instil confidence in all Canadians, those who are working and paying for these benefits, employers and those who are in the unfortunate position of having to collect benefits. Measures are needed to tighten the eligibility for benefit. More effort must be put into finding jobs for the unemployed, and the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act must be improved for the sake of those rightfully receiving unemployment benefits.
Additional provisions must be enacted to curb abuses of the unemployment insurance system. One method that would accomplish this would be to base eligibility on both earnings, and the number of weeks employed during the full 52 weeks of the previous year. This provision would have the advantage of removing from the unemployment insurance rolls those seasonal workers who earn as much for working several months of the year as do some workers who work a full year and are laid off. This amendment, I feel, would bring a semblance of equity into the act, which is long overdue in the eyes of the Canadian public, employees and employers. I think most members could tell stories about people in their constituencies whose incomes are very healthy indeed. Because these people earn their income in less than a full year, they are entitled to go on unemployment insurance for the remainder of the year when they are not working. Technically, I suppose, these are not abuses because the act allows it to happen. Nonetheless, one can see that this is unfair. It creates a great deal of resentment on the part of those not so fortunate as to take advantage of the act in this way.
Secondly, the UIC must put more effort into the quick and effective reabsorption of unemployed workers into the labour force. This it can do only with a fully integrated program with the Department of Manpower. We have all, undoubtedly, as members of parliament, had brought to our attention numerous cases of the damage done to our constituents by the inability of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the Manpower department to provide assistance to the jobless in finding employment. In some cases this has been caused by lack of integration of programs and, on the other hand, by duplication of programs. These anomalies could be erased somewhat if the Manpower department and the Unemployment Insurance Commission were to merge and if the unemployed receiving benefits were counselled on a regular basis.

October 29, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
The final point I should like to make regarding the present amendments to this act is on the question of administration. Even if the legislation were to contain all the amendments proposed on both sides of the House, I say that unless the act is well administered it is of no practical use. During the last couple of years the administration of the present act has been a source of numerous complaints. I have been a member of this House since 1972, and-I am sure other members will agree-by far the largest percentage of our constituency mail involves complaints about the payment of UIC claims. Surely, some simplification of procedures and forms can be instituted in the department to allow the average citizen to complete the requirements of the department without such difficulty. As it stands now, you must practically have had a higher education to fulfill the requirements of the commission.
I have outlined some of the features of which I think the government should take serious note. These are not paltry objections but, rather, ones which concern all Canadians, especially all Canadian taxpayers who are confused and resentful of the government's policies and the objects of the unemployment insurance scheme. I hope and trust that the government will give my views and the views of my colleagues their careful consideration, and that our joint discussions will result in a more equitable unemployment insurance scheme. As I said at the beginning, the majority of Canadians support a true insurance scheme which protects those who, through no fault of their own, are unemployed. By the same token, abuses made possible by mismanagement in the past and poor administration have built up a huge reservoir of resentment. This resentment must be removed. These abuses have deteriorated the sense of worth and purpose in this country and they have deteriorated the work ethic. The side effects have been serious.
The difficulty will be resolved, I suggest, if the government gives serious consideration to our suggestions. If it does, I suggest that this bill will receive quick and easy passage through the committee stage and all Canadians will benefit. But until we see a willingness on the part of the government to listen, I can only echo the remarks of my colleague from Hamilton West. We intend to vote against this legislation on second reading. Nevertheless, we hope that the committee deliberations will encourage us to vote in favour of the bill on third reading.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I put on the record this afternoon some of my thoughts concerning the UIC program and this bill. Surely amendments brought forward at present and in future are designed to streamline and clarify the law. We need to cut down abuses and to shift some of the benefits of the program from those who are casually attached to the labour force to those who are permanently attached to the labour force. This bill deserves the support of the members from all parties, for we must help those who need help most.
I am disturbed to hear some of the bitter attacks made on the UIC both inside and outside this House. What is the alternative to UIC? I wonder if municipalities in parts of the country where unemployment is high have the tax base to fund the type of welfare program which would be needed in the absence of UIC. I suspect that the stroneest supporters of UIC are municipal councillors across Canada.
I hope I can make clear that we are considering some of the first amendments which will be brought down, for the act will be under continuous review. In future, there will be additional amendments to the UIC program which will need consideration. I certainly support the amendments presently being brought forward. These amendments are designed to eliminate the inequities and complexities inherent in the act. I agree with the hon. member who spoke previously: the act is complex and difficult to administer. These complexities and difficulties have given rise to many borderline cases, as the act does not always define clearly who is or who is not eligible for benefit. This lack of clarity has meant that people in our constituency offices, our staffs in the House and people in UIC offices, must spend much of their time dealing with marginal cases. Sometimes it is difficult to determine who qualifies for benefits.
I am particularly pleased with the amendment designed to eliminate disincentives-disincentives which, perhaps, may be associated with the present legislation. It is essential for the UIC program to be credible; its success depends to a large extent on public support and public opinion. I trust that these amendments will do much to increase public support.
I am concerned about the treatment of people leaving jobs voluntarily. It is apparent that some people engage in job misconduct. They are subsequently fired, only to receive benefits. I am concerned, also, about the high percentage of people refusing job opportunities. The present bill deals with these matters. Surely it should be the basic approach of the UIC program that we shall provide income to those who are unemployed against their will, provided that they have qualified for entitlement to benefits through previous attachment to the work force. That, surely, is what the amendments and the bill are all about.
I do not have as much difficulty with the amendments to the act as some members, in terms of eliminating from the act some of the provisions covered in other social legislation. If we approve of the amendments put forward, our Unemployment Insurance Act will be improved considerably. These amendments provide a greater amount of assurance against unemployment, as opposed to compensating someone with retirement income or the many other things factored into it. In this manner, assurance against unemployment will lead to stronger public support, in effect, this means the UIC act will be considerably easier to administer.
I am particularly pleased that introduced in the amendments is the payments of improved sick benefits. Nearly every other member of this House, plus myself, made representations on this amendment. Some of the most difficult and time-consuming cases we as members of parliament deal with are those pregnancy leaves where difficulties after the birth occur, or where a person has been sick, returns to work and gets sick again. Experience seems to indicate that the second illness may be more severe and prolonged than the initial one. This works great hardship on the individual concerned. Many times these people have no other income protection for sickness. It is a great step forward that improved more flexible sick benefits are included in the amendments.

October 29, 1975

If I may, I wish to raise another issue in which I am keenly interested. Who are the unemployed? In this area, we should be more definitive when answering that question. My understanding is that a survey is being conducted on 30,000 households to find out who is classified as being unemployed. There should be no quarrel with that number because statistically the number is large. Such a survey should yield a very accurate sample and response. However, what I take issue with is the question asked: Are you unemployed, and are you actively looking for work? It seems that many government policies are set and based upon the unemployment rate. In fact, many of our economic policies also rely upon the unemployment act. For this reason, we should have more detailed information as to who are the unemployed.
My suggestion is to change the survey so that the response indicates what percentage of the people unemployed are the principal wage earners of the household. That would be a very different figure from the total unemployed. In this survey we should also be exploring why these people are unemployed, whether these people left the job or whether these people are a new entry into the work force. That is a particularly significant statistic. We should also determine whether these people were laid off on a recall basis, or laid off without any recall possibility. That type of statistic would further define who are the unemployed, and possibly where we should be directing more of the benefits. I would like to see also, the weekly survey turn up information that will identify the number of new entries into the work force, the number of people who had a major attachment to the work force, and are now unemployed, and the number of people who had a rather casual attachment to the work force.
During this debate there has been a lot of talk concerning the over-all administration of unemployment insurance benefits. I have also heard that more emphasis should be placed on the role played by the Department of Manpower. In the offices where the Unemployment Insurance Commission works extremely well and UlC is extremely well handled, UIC is in fact performing some of the functions that we would ordinarily expect the Department of Manpower to perform. If it is in order, I wish to commend the Unemployment Insurance Commission office in Barrie which services part of my constituency. An activity that I think UIC officers should be performing, supported strongly by Manpower, is monitoring the job situation very carefully so that the UIC officers are aware of any significant lay-offs prior to such a happening.
At the time of the lay-off, the UIC officers are present along with the union and management people to sort out all the difficulties in establishing claims. Most important, by monitoring the work opportunities as closely as the UIC officers do, the UIC officers know ahead of time exactly when the callbacks are scheduled and where other opportunities exist. Therefore, those on benefits are very quickly directed to other opportunities. This drastically cuts down the number on benefits and gives the appearance that the UIC operation is sincerely concerned with employment rather than just the payment of benefits to the unemployed.
I know there are great variations across Canada in the nature of communities and problems. In some areas there
Unemployment Insurance Act
is a multitude of employment opportunities, with a great variety and number of industries. In another area there may be only one employer. The program should provide that where there is little or no alternate employment after a certain period of time, it is proper that Manpower retraining be supported by the UIC benefit. That would be a better use of the money and the individual's time than to be on benefit without any real opportunity of obtaining work in the near future. I support the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) who on a number of occasions has advocated that the name "unemployment insurance" be changed to "employment insurance." That would be a worth-while amendment to be considered at some time in the future.
I wonder a bit about the amendment with regard to the situation where people lose jobs due to self-initiated misconduct, voluntary leaving without just cause, or refusal to apply for or accept a suitable job. The bill proposes lengthening from three to six weeks the period to become eligible for benefits, and in fact losing benefits for three weeks. Possibly the onus should be on the individual to prove that one of these three situations is not the case. If he is able to prove that, he should have the same benefit as anyone else under the act. However, the onus should be on him to establish the fact that he did not leave because of misconduct, that there was just cause for him to leave for some very valid reason or that he could not accept a job.
Members opposite have been proposing a 12-week period. The amendment speaks of an additional three weeks. I believe the entire onus should be on the individual to establish whether in fact he is entitled to regular benefits. Having done so, they should be available to him.
I support the amendment to delete the provision with regard to advance payments. I do not say that because it may or may not be an incentive to get back into the work force. I do not know whether you do an individual a favour by giving him an advance payment. The money may be claimed back after the person has spent it. I have seen cases where this has caused tremendous hardship. Certainly, many hours of my time are spent dealing with people who have had an advance payment, it is claimed back and they have neither the money nor the credit to get it. It would be better if they had not received the money in the first place.
I support the approach in the bill which, in effect, decreases benefits and increases the difficulty of getting benefits for those marginally attached to the work force, and increases benefits and decreases the difficulty in getting benefits for those who have a continuous attachment to the work force. Another amendment that I am glad to see speaks to the problem of social insurance. I am sure that many of the numbers we hear from time to time of people obtaining social insurance are exaggerated. Nevertheless, we must acknowledge that there are abuses and that people do get social insurance improperly. This is a problem that does no one a service; everyone is hurt by it, the employer and the employee.
Those people obtaining social insurance numbers by illegal means will in most cases end up in employment which is paying the minimum wage or even less. I hope

October 29, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
that the social insurance number provision in here will help correct this problem. I would like to have the assurance that this provision would, if possible, almost totally correct any abuse where people might be able to get social insurance numbers improperly.
I see my time is just about up, and I would like to conclude by commending the amendments in the legislation. Speaking to the illness benefits, as everyone in the House knows, the present provision provides that illness benefits are payable only during the initial benefit period of a claim and are not payable during the re-establishment or extended benefit periods of any claim. It goes on in terms of regulations respecting the difference between a major attachment and a minor attachment. I find no difficulty with that part, but I think the major provision, whereby illness benefits are only payable during the initial benefit period, really works a tremendous hardship on a lot of people. We must all be aware of people who have been injured, who have been working with Workmen's Compensation rehabilitation programs, and so on, and have gone back to work only to find they have a recurrence of the illness or their injury is not sufficiently healed. In fact, they may well be off work longer the second time than they were the first time.
Many of these people have no other income protection for this eventuality, and because they cannot file a claim I think it works a good deal of hardship upon them, even if people had only used a small amount of their eligibility in terms of their 15 weeks. So by making it more flexible and allowing more latitude, this is a social measure I strongly support. I hope all members in the House share my opinion. To extend the period during which the eligibility for benefits may be established, to persons who have left the labour force for periods of time for reasons clearly beyond their control, like serious sickness or serious injury with resulting disability, seems to me to call for the unanimous consent of the House.
The other point I mentioned previously and I would like to comment on it again. I am an engineer, not a doctor like my good friend from Halton (Mr. Philbrook). It has always amazed me that the medical profession can predict the accurate date of birth. Whether they are as accurate as they pretend to be, I have no idea, but most certainly they all do in many cases where birth has in fact been premature, so that a person did not have an opportunity earlier to lay claim for that eight-week period. It seems that sometimes these women have serious difficulty and the six-week period afterwards does not adequately cover that problem. By taking the 14-week period and making it more flexible as to when a person can take advantage of it is surely a fair thing that should be available to any woman who has need of pregnancy leave.
I conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying I am pleased the minister has brought the bill forward and that these amendments are contained in it. I would hope that the bill is only stage one of a review of the act, because it is a large act and affects many people across Canada. I think it is worthy of being continuously under review.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt in anyone's mind that the unemployment insurance law is one of those measures which has to be reviewed by parliament from time to time. The present

Unemployment Insurance Act obviously has within it certain inherent weaknesses. I imagine there is not a member of this House who has not been called upon to deal with problems arising from those weaknesses, shortcomings and anomalies. Indeed, not a week goes by without our having to deal with questions arising from the administration of this statute.
So there is no doubt in anybody's mind that the present law needs tightening up. Certain of the provisions in the bill now before us address themselves to the shortcomings and anomalies to which I have referred. If that were the extent of the legislation, the bill would receive easy and speedy passage because we are all agreed on the need to take whatever steps may be necessary to prevent a small minority in our society abusing this legislation.
I am glad to see that some of the punitive sections of the act are being tightened up and that steps are to be taken to reduce, at least, the scope of the abuses which take place frequently. As I say, if this were the extent of the bill, it would secure an easy passage through the House. Obviously, our job as members of parliament would be made easier because the workload in our offices would be reduced. The most extensive problems we have to deal with, especially in our constituency offices, relate to unemployment insurance.
What concerns me are those provisions in the bill which lean heavily upon two groups in our society which already suffer most as a consequence of inflation. I refer specifically to old age pensioners and to low income earners with dependent children. First, let us take the case of low-income earners with dependent children. The bill proposes to end the secial privilege they now enjoy under the statute and to give them the same benefits as anybody else receives, notwithstanding the fact that their obligations are greater than those of others.
I listened to the argument put forward by the minister when he introduced the bill with respect to the new amendments to the Family Allowance Act which provide for increased family allowance payments. The minister suggested that these arrangements would look after the particular group to which I have just referred. He used much the same argument with regard to the position of old age pensioners. But let us take the case of an unemployment insurance recipient who has five dependent children. After this bill becomes law, he will receive the same benefits as everybody else-66% per cent of his income as opposed to the 75 per cent he formerly received. He would be entitled to receive $100 a month, in round figures, in family allowance benefits. But that sum in no way covers the expenses he must incur in providing food, clothing, shelter and other necessities of life for his family. Why should the low income earner with a large family be discriminated against in this way? Why lean on him? This is precisely what the bill attempts to do.
In my province we have the highest rate of unemployment in the country, the second lowest per capita income in the country, the highest rate of inflation in the country and the largest families in the country. Given these statistics, the bill is going to take a particularly heavy toll of the 18 per cent of the work force currently unemployed in the
October 29, 1975

province of Newfoundland. The majority of the people who are unemployed, statistics tell us, are the very group that the bill will lean on most heavily-the group with dependent children.
The minister has done a great job of administering the LIP program. He has involved members of parliament in LIP decision-making and as a result has taken away some of the administrative burden from his own shoulders. He has involved us all in the LIP program. But I would tell him that this is not the way to reform the Unemployment Insurance Act. This is not the kind of reform that the members of this House want. Indeed, I would say that the majority of the members of the House, if they voted according to their conscience, would vote against that particular provision in the bill. The people who will be affected by it the most are those who live in provinces where unemployment is highest, namely, the Atlantic provinces and the province of Quebec.
Coincidentally, these are the provinces where the largest families reside. According to statistics, families are larger in Quebec, Newfoundland and the Atlantic provinces generally than any other part of Canada. These are the people who will be hurt the most by this particular provision in the bill, and I hope that before the bill is given third reading the minister will reconsider it.
While it is true to say that inflation hurts us all, it hurts the low income earner the most. I reject the argument that because a man is receiving unemployment insurance the state has discharged its obligation to him. Notwithstanding that he may be receiving unemployment insurance and family allowance benefits, the fact is that he has to devote a disproportionately greater amount of his disposable income, the little that he has, to the purchase of food. Food inflation in Canada is taking its highest toll at the present time.
A man in receipt of $75 a week unemployment insurance and $25 a week family allowance, which means he would have to have five children, has $100 a week to buy food, clothing, shelter, transportation and education for himself, his wife and his five dependent children. I ask members of this House, given the situation that we have in Canada today, with high food prices, high fuel prices, with the cost of everything disproportionately high as a result of the inflation that we are suffering, to try to imagine how anyone can live adequately and provide their children with an adequate diet on $100 a week.
For this reason, I hope the minister will reconsider this unjust and iniquitous provision of the bill. It will do great injustice to this particular group in society which is already suffering the most-the low income earner with a large family. He cannot help it if he is unemployed. He does not want to be unemployed. He did not bring on the monetary and fiscal situation in Canada that has created the recession we are now experiencing-7.3 per cent unemployment nationally, in excess of 10 per cent in the Atlantic provinces and 18 per cent in Newfoundland-but he has to suffer the consequences of it. Why should we increase the price that he has to pay by reducing the little extra benefit that parliament in its wisdom put into the act to take account of the extra burden he has to bear owing to his low income and the large family that he has to support?
Unemployment Insurance Act
The other group that equally cries out for justice is the old age pensioners. They suffer even more because their income is fixed. I know their pensions are now indexed, which does help them in some small way, but nevertheless they watch their limited pensions being reduced in spending power monthly by an inflationary situation in Canada with which we have yet to come to grips. Take the case of the old age pensioner, man or woman, whether they worked all their lives or made a contribution in some other way: the fact of the matter is that in this bill we are adding to their burden by eliminating them from the unemployment insurance rolls. Secondly, and equally unjustly and iniquitously, we are removing the incentive that we presently provide these people, with their accumulated fund of knowledge and experience, to stay in the work force.
Many old age pensioners in this country write to members of parliament pointing out that they fail to understand how their representatives here can consider putting such a provision as this in an unemployment insurance bill, let alone pass it into law. The old age pensioners of this country are entitled to unemployment insurance as of right because they have paid for it. Their desire is to continue to be part of the work force. Obviously, the provisions of the act cannot apply to old age pensioners who are no longer part of the work force, and no one would want the act to apply to them. But what about the thousands of old age pensioners in Canada who are forced to retire at the age of 65? They want to continue to work, they register for employment with Manpower, and they rightly feel, having paid into this scheme all their working lives, that they are entitled to its benefits while waiting for the government to find them new employment. Yet these are the people we are eliminating from the unemployment insurance rolls of this country. This is unjust, unfair and cruel, and I hope the minister and his government will reconsider this provision.
The third aspect of this bill that has disturbed me is the changing of the benchmark, which will have the concomitant effect of increasing unemployment insurance deductions. Once again, who will have to bear the heaviest burden of this increase? Who will have to pay the highest price? Who will have to suffer most as a consequence? The answer to these questions is, the low income earner of this country and the person on fixed income who spends such a disproportionate amount of his disposable income on food, clothing and shelter and who sees his income dwindling still further by having to pay increased unemployment insurance contributions. This will be the situation if the provisions of this bill go through the House. These are the three aspects of the bill that bother me.
I hope hon. members will sufficiently impress the minister so that he will reconsider this measure in this period of high inflation and high unemployment. We all hope there will come a time somewhere down the road when we will have inflation and unemployment controlled at acceptable levels. Perhaps then, and only then, should we consider bringing in this punitive type of legislation which will rest so heavily on the working poor, pensioners and those on fixed incomes in this country.

October 29, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act

I should like to begin by commenting on some of the specific amendments proposed in Bill C-69. I think it is proper and sensible that sponsors of Local Initiatives and Local Employment Assistance Programs should now become eligible for coverage and benefits. It has always seemed incongruous to me that governments should provide funds for the purpose of alleviating unemployment at the local level, and then penalize those who take the initiative to sponsor such programs by making them ineligible for unemployment benefits. If, indeed, the government places importance on job creation for the unemployed in the creation and management of projects, then it has no choice but to bring in this kind of amendment. It will now afford equal treatment to both the individual worker and the individual sponsor under LIP and LEAP projects vis-a-vis unemployment insurance coverage.
With reference to the amendment in respect of coverage of workers 65 years of age and over, I must say that I, too, have some reservations. I can agree quite readily that anyone between age 65 and 70 who is receiving old age security, the guaranteed income supplement and Canada or Quebec Pension Plan benefits should certainly be ineligible to receive unemployment insurance benefits over an extended period of time. However, there are many people who choose, through desire or necessity, to continue active employment after age 65, and while old age security benefits are payable upon application to everyone who has attained age 65, that does not apply to the guaranteed income supplement or Canada Pension Plan benefits.

speechtext:
I will try. Therefore, it would seem to me that people who are not receiving a guaranteed income supplement should be eligible to pay into and receive benefits from the unemployment insurance fund. May I remind this House that many people between age 65 and 70 are still supporting depend-

ent children or other relatives who may well be attending university or other institutions of higher learning or who may, through sickness or accident, be unable to assist themselves. I do not believe that any government action, especially action by a Liberal government, should deprive such people of the expectations and historical rights which they have had under this act. I would, therefore, urge that this proposed amendment be redrafted in such a way as to make an exception of those whose attachment to the labour force and whose need for benefit is demonstrated to local officials of the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
I find it necessary, also, to say a few words regarding the amendments, in respect of the manner and conditions for claiming benefits. While the present legislation provides authority for the commission to regulate the manner in which a claim for benefit may be made, and while such procedure may be contrary to the basic principle that a regulation may only purport to explain the law or help in administering it, it must be pointed out that legislation is much more rigid than regulation. Therefore, it may well be that experience will prove that legislating the manner and conditions for claiming benefits is so rigid that no allowance is made for special circumstances. If, however, the legislation can be drafted in such a way as to allow for some flexibility in the administration of the act, then I have no objection to it.
I believe the amendments under the clauses dealing with the extension of the qualifying period and the benefit period are beneficial and sensible and I give them my full support. There is, however, one disincentive to work contained in the act to which this bill does not seem to address itself. I refer to the disentitlement of a claimant who takes a part-time job while still receiving unemployment insurance benefits-a job that lasts four or more weeks. After working for four weeks, the claim is discontinued and the claimant finds himself in a position of not being eligible to continue drawing benefits, even though through his own initiative and desire to work he has saved the Unemployment Insurance Commission the payment of four weeks' benefits. The incentive here is to encourage such people not to accept part-time work while receiving benefits. I suspect this is an oversight in the drafting of the bill. I strongly urge that new legislation be proposed to allow claimants to take such short-term employment and, at the end of this employment, be able once again to continue to receive benefits and to renew their claims.
The interpretation of the regulations at present seriously affects one particular group of prospective claimants in the province of New Brunswick. I do not know whether the same applies in other provinces, but several instances of this faulty interpretation of the regulations have been brought to my attention. It is simply this: in the province of New Brunswick, teachers' contracts are dated to coincide with the dates of the school year; that is to say, from July 1 to the following June 30.
Because of the interpretation given by the commission, any individual who signs a teachers's contract in New Brunswick is automatically disentitled to unemployment insurance benefits from July 1 of the year in which the contract is signed, even though the actual pay period for teachers in New Brunswick does not commence until September 1. Consequently, it is entirely possible in fact, it
October 29, 1975

has happened that legitimate claimants have been deprived of unemployment insurance benefits for the months of July and August because they signed a contract while they were receiving unemployment insurance benefits to which they had every entitlement. I might point out that this applies even if an individual signed a contract in the middle of August; he would then be required to pay back all the benefits he received from July 1 to that time.
Of course, I am not referring to teachers who are on continuing contracts from year to year, but to those who are just entering the profession for the first time or are just returning to it after a period of absence. I suspect that this is an administrative blunder made simply by people who do not really understand the peculiar circumstances of the situation, and I sincerely hope this anomaly will be corrected without waiting for the passage of this bill. I need not remind the House that teachers very strongly opposed being included in the unemployment insurance scheme. But since they have been included, and rightly so, no teacher should be deprived of benefits to which he or she has a just claim.
I stress that this is not a complaint against the local officials of the UIC in the area which I have the honour to represent. In fact, I have found the manager of the local unemployment insurance office to be extremely well informed, very capable and most co-operative; I do not want to pass up this opportunity of saying a good word for the oft maligned bureaucrats whose responsibility it is to administer the laws of the country which have a direct effect on the lives of so many of us.
I hoped that Bill C-69 might have included some provision to take into the unemployment insurance scheme seasonal, self-employed persons other than fishermen. There are many individual truckers, for instance particularly in the areas of the country hardest hit by unemployment, who can only work part time because their business is dependent on other business operations whose nature is also seasonal. Because of this, many of them are left with the necessity of supporting themselves and their families as well as making payments on equipment during fairly extended periods of time when they have no income.
I respectfully suggest that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) give more consideration to this problem than it has received to date. This is not to suggest that fishermen who are already covered by the act should not be entitled to the benefits they receive but, rather, that there are other groups of seasonal, selfemployed workers who find themselves in very much the same situation as fishermen. In my opinion, the government should be prepared to offer them the same kind of benefits as any other group in our society.
Having said all that, I want it borne in mind that this bill will receive my full support because it does go a long way toward correcting anomalies and injustices which have appeared through the administration of the 1971 act. It has consistently been the policy of successive Liberal governments in this country that government must be prepared to help those in our society who, through no fault of their own, find themselves in the position of being unable to help themselves. This, indeed, is the basic princi-
Unemployment Insurance Act
pie underlying all the social legislation passed by the governments of MacKenzie King, Louis St. Laurent, Lester Pearson and Pierre Elliott Trudeau. I am convinced that this is the spirit of liberalism to which the minister has addressed himself in this bill.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure for me to participate in today's debate on Bill C-69 along with members from all sides of the House, and I welcome the presence of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) throughout this debate. Let me say at the outset that, despite my many apprehensions concerning the government's management of the Unemployment Insurance Act, I am in complete agreement with the retention of an adequate wage-loss compensation plan. I fully support the true concept of unemployment insurance.
Unfortunately, however, the plan as we now know it bears little resemblance to what it was set out to be in the original act, namely, a plan of insurance for those whose salary or wages are suddenly interrupted through an unexpected job loss. Bill C-69 does little, if anything, to regain this proper perspective of an actual insurance program. Because benefits are not rigorously tied to employment records, the insurance principle is subverted and the whole scheme becomes largely a plan of social welfare and wage distribution rather than one of unemployment insurance. Because of the high and extremely appealing benefit rate structure, the risk of unemployment is no longer an integral factor in the decision to work or not to work. The traditional work ethic has been seriously jeopardized at a time in our economic life when the country can ill afford it.
What is needed, Mr. Speaker, is a redefinition of the work week and the benefits structure in order that these basic principles can, be put back into practice. Without accepting this philosophy, not only in theory but in practice, almost anything the government attempts to do in amending the Unemployment Insurance Act becomes useless. So, in spite of a sprinkled hint of reform here and there, the main thing that can be said about the introduction of Bill C-69 is that its provisions are superfluous to the real problem confronting unemployment insurance today.
In fact, I may even be accused of being overly generous to the government in this regard. On closer examination it would appear that the main thrust of this bill is in the adjustment of the benchmark, the point at which the government agrees to contribute to the fund. This is clearly a regressive step in that it greatly increases the burden of premium payments to employer and employee, yet without an adequate distinction between those who are high-risk insurees and those who are low risk. Surely, this
8674

October 29, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
should be basic to any organized plan of insurance, unemployment or otherwise.
What would make far greater sense would be a formula for reducing, on a percentage basis, the amount of premiums paid by those who compile a steady and continuous employment record and who are thus proven to be low risks as potential claimants of benefits. Such a system, if implemented, would be far more equitable than the one we have at present, in that those whose contributions are most reliable-indeed, those who are most conscientious- would not be continually forced to carry those who are not. Admittedly, this would not eliminate all imbalances but it would certainly be a good deal fairer than the present scheme, especially in view of the fact that the government proposes to raise the premium payments of employees through the new benchmark proviso in Bill C-69.
In the same vein, there is need to look at retirement benefits under the unemployment insurance program. As it stands now, one who has been actively employed all his or her working life, one who has contributed the maximum amount in the way of premiums, has little to look forward to in the way of a deserved retirement award. It is time for an adequate retirement clause to be incorporated into the act so that this inequity may be rectified. This would be a welcome addition to Bill C-69.
The very fact that the government deemed it necessary to adjust the benchmark is in itself a self-admission of failure in its handling of the unemployment insurance program. Things have clearly got out of hand and determined action is needed to straighten out the situation. Unfortunately, we can see nothing in Bill C-69 toward this end. It is another case of pulling a drowning man out of the water, then tossing him in again without first teaching him how to swim.
I have already noted that because benefits are not sufficiently connected to employment records, and because benefit rate structures are so appealing, the tendency to a disincentive to work becomes apparent. This obvious shortcoming could be overcome, Mr. Speaker, by redefining the work week and the benefit structure. Where in Bill C-69 do we see a concrete proposal to abandon the work week in favour of a more reliable work year? Rather than calculating benefits on the basis of weekly insurable earnings, why not calculate them on a yearly basis? Initial eligibility need not be affected, but the initial benefit rate could be calculated on both earnings and the number of weeks employed in the previous year.
If an employee had worked a full year prior to a claim, then his benefit rate would be substantially higher than a worker who had a much shorter attachment to the labour force. This scheme would have the obvious advantage of providing work incentives and it would guarantee that the original insurance principles of unemployment insurance were upheld.
I do not wish to go on record, Mr. Speaker, as being opposed to all the provisions of Bill C-69. Some of these amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act may prove useful and are worthy of mention. They include, first, extension of the period during which a claim can be made and benefits received for those suffering temporary disability or those who are on special training courses and, 
second, extension of the time for claiming from 15 weeks to 25 for those entitled to sickness benefits.
It would have been equally constructive to tie maternity benefits to sickness benefits because of the difficulties and unfairness in the calculation of maternity benefits due to the use of the confinement date. I would suggest a set period for maternity benefits or, better still, including as a sickness claim the length, depending upon the doctor's estimate, of temporary disability.
With regard to the increase from three to six weeks of the period of disqualification for those who quit, are fired or refuse suitable employment, one hopes that this extended disqualification period will not only serve to differentiate between those who quit or are fired and those who are laid off or terminated for reasons beyond their control, but will also provide scope for more thorough investigation into the job search being conducted by claimants before they are allowed to collect any benefits at all.
It is a well known fact that many are receiving benefits who, although unemployed, are not conducting an honest job search. In some cases such claimants have no intention whatsoever of working. They are ripping off the system at the expense of honest taxpayers and are being allowed to get away with it. I know of cases where claimants have collected benefits for extended periods of time without ever being asked if they were conducting active job searches. For example, job search reports appear to be sent only to a random selection of claimants. Clearly, a more comprehensive investigative machinery is required. With six weeks available before some claims become payable, it is imperative that all such claimants prove to the Unemployment Insurance Commission that they are actively seeking employment. The burden of proof must be on the claimant, and the standard of proof must be raised.
One way in which this kind of reform can be more easily accomplished is through much further decentralization of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Lack of decentralization has been one of the prime failings of the operation for many years, and I am indeed sorry that no definite _ amendments are present in Bill C-69 relating to this problem.
I believe that greater understanding between UIC officers and individual claimants, most of whose claims are perfectly legitimate, could be achieved through decentralization. Similarly, there can be no doubt concerning the need for higher quality performance at all levels. Such an undertaking, that is, decentralization, could also offer additional impetus to the promotion of relocation of those among the unemployed who find it impossible to locate work within their own area or territory.
The commission must be encouraged to develop more uniformity in its decisions. Most members of parliament deal with a great many UIC cases and most are acutely aware of the tragic lack of uniformity which mars the performance of most offices. I do not refer simply to the lack of uniformity between offices, but within offices as well. There is a multitude of unfortunate cases on record in which identical claims were processed in differing manners and the outcome of the claims differed considerably. While I have emphasized that more vigilance must be
October 29, 1975

exercised in weeding out those who abuse unemployment insurance, I wish also to reiterate that those who are honest, legitimate and needy claimants must be treated with greater dispatch and in a more uniform manner. As I said previously, this can be most easily accomplished through decentralization and through stronger ties between the commission and Canada Manpower centres.
I recognize that last year the department undertook to increase co-operation between these two agencies. This co-operation has yet to bear fruit. In other words, those who collect benefits because they are unable to find jobs have been given little help by the Unemployment Insurance Commission. While it is true that counselling on job placement is given to most clients, it is felt that a more active role must be undertaken to locate jobs for those unable to find work.
Bill C-69 is a mere drop in the bucket. A comprehensive investigation into the whole scheme of unemployment insurance is overdue. With Bill C-69 as an example of the inability of the government to cope with the problem, perhaps it is time for an objective investigation in order that some truly effective recommendations may be placed before us.
I note that there is no reference in Bill C-69 to occasional workers employed in the agricultural industry. This is a very troublesome problem, particularly in southern Ontario. A heavy percentage of these people are relatives, friends and sometimes neighbours of farmers who may work for one or perhaps two months at a time, thus working over 25 days and earning more than $250. A great majority of these people have no intention of availing themselves of benefits or of taking other jobs, yet they are forced to pay premiums into a fund from which they will never, or seldom, collect. As these workers have no interest in unemployment insurance, it would only be logical that they be exempt from paying premiums if they should so choose. It would be far more equitable to give them the option of contributing or opting out, rather than requiring mandatory payments as is the case now.
I should like to add a few words about seasonal workers of another sort entirely, those in industries who earn better than average incomes over an eight or nine-month period and are well aware in advance of their idle months. Many of these workers earn in excess of $15,000, and even $20,000, during the period they are actively employed. Why, then, are they permitted to collect unemployment insurance benefits?
Once again we return to the basic principle of unemployment insurance, and that is as insurance against job and income loss. In these particular cases jobs are not lost; they are only temporarily suspended. Perhaps more important, there is no unnecessary financial hardship imposed upon the individual worker. In accordance with these facts, it is my suggestion that a ceiling be placed on yearly earnings for which one is eligible to collect unemployment insurance, provided that the job interruption is on a temporary basis.
