subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I read the speech of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) which began debate on this bill, I was struck by the tremendous difference between it and the speech made by the former minister of manpower and immigration who introduced amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act in April, 1971. This minister s speech was apologetic, offensive and pessimistic. He obviously forsees a long-term, persistent and high rate of unemployment. The former minister was hopeful, optimistic and obviously expected that the rate of unemployment which prevailed at that time could be drastically reduced.
The best example of the difference to which I have referred can be seen by comparing the parts of the two speeches which deal with the point at which the percentage of unemployment brings the government into the funding of the unemployment insurance scheme. On Monday, October 27, when introducing the bill the present minister referred to the 1971 proposals. He said:
At that time, a threshold of 4 per cent unemployment was set as the level above which the government would assume the additional costs for unemployment insurance benefits.
That 4 per cent threshold was related to the economic conditions in the decade preceding 1970. The basic financing principle continues to hold true. Nevertheless, under social insurance principles, normal cost under the unemployment insurance program should be financed as much as possible through contributions from employers and employees.
He went on to say:
Applying this formula in 1976, the benchmark for the year will be about 5.6 per cent, a level based on average monthly rates of unemployment in the eight years preceding June 30, 1975.
Later he said:
the premium change, if the proposed amendments are fully implemented as of January 1, 1976, we can expect a net saving of $170 million in 1976 at a 7 per cent rate of unemployment.
In other words, the minister accepts 7 per cent unemployment as normal. In fact, we have had higher than 7 per cent for almost a year, and the predictions for the next couple of years are that it will go still higher. What did the former minister say when he introduced his amendments in 1971? He said:
29669-6S'/2
October 29, 1975

Unemployment Insurance Act
Since the figure of 4 per cent has attracted a good deal of attention, I imagine somebody is going to suggest that the government has determined 4 per cent to be an acceptable rate of unemployment in Canada. Well, it is not my criterion. Like everybody else, I believe the acceptable rate of unemployment is the least possible rate.
He continued:
-We have used the 4 per cent figure because 4 per cent according to our computer estimates, triggers the government's contribution to the fund at a realistic level.
Then he said the government would have every inducement, if unemployment was at 6 per cent, to take measures to cut back the rate of employment because it would cost the government hundreds of millions of dollars to help finance unemployment insurance benefits. He was much too optimistic. Since 1971, the average rate of unemployment has only been below 5 per cent for one month. In 1971, the average rate of unemployment was 6.4 per cent; in 1972, it was 6.3 per cent; in 1974 it was 5.4 per cent; and each month this year it has been over 7 per cent, the highest rate of unemployment since 1961.
If there is one thing that the columnists are agreed upon, it is that the government's proposed anti-inflation measures will force the rate of unemployment even higher. They are divided on the scale, but most agree that the rate of employment will rise between one-half per cent and Wi per cent in 1976. Because of the government's mistaken economic policies, the unemployment rate is expected to reach 8 per cent or more.
In 1971 the government had to put $700 million into the fund because the unemployment rate was more than 4 per cent and the contribution of employers and employees only met the expenses of the fund up to a rate of 4 per cent. This year, the cost to the people of Canada is likely to be $3'/2 billion, and in 1976 it is estimated it will cost $5 billion.
Under the existing legislation, $2 billion of the 1975 pay-out would come from employer-employee contributions, and $l'/2 billion from the government. The government is committed to absorb the extra costs of unemployment beyond 4 per cent under the present legislation, but it will have difficulty explaining that kind of deficit to the Canadian people. It cannot admit, of course, that the deficit is to a large extent the result of its own stupid economic policy, so in typical Liberal fashion it has found an ingenious way to solve the problem; it will tax the ordinary citizen. The unemployment insurance premium of workers will be raised from $1.40 per $100 to $1.60 or $1.70, so about $500 million will be shifted on to the backs of employers and employees in 1976.
On June 30, 1975, the Financial Times estimated that premiums are likely to be closer to $2 per $100 and that the government will be shifting closer to $800 million on to employers and employees in 1976. As the unemployment rate goes up, then the potential pay-out of the government goes up as well. In other words, if the ordinary citizen pays more, the government pays less. We should keep in mind that, like so many other tax proposals of Liberal governments, this proposal is especially regressive. The Unemployment Insurance Commission could affect all incomes at the same rate. There is a fairly low ceiling on contributions, so premiums represent a bigger proportion of the income of lower paid workers than of higher paid workers. The increase will come primarily out of the pockets of the lower paid workers, and there are more of them.
We oppose the minister's present proposals. As I have said, we think this is the wrong tax put on the wrong people at the wrong time. Right now, when the rate of inflation shows no sign of abating and when the cost of living is so high after the enormous increases of the past two or three years, the government wants to tax precisely those who can least afford to pay. As I said earlier, when the former minister talked about the government bearing the cost of unemployment insurance when unemployment rose above the 4 per cent threshold, unemployment was much lower. In 1971, the unemployment rate was 6.4 per cent; in 1972 it was 6.3 per cent; in 1973 it was 5.6 per cent; in 1974 it was 5.4 per cent; but this year it is over 7 per cent. Surely, the government should not now ask the people of this country to pay more unemployment insurance to relieve the effects of unemployment which the government itself created.
There is something even more pernicious in the current proposal. By making everyone pay this extra tax, the government is saying that all workers, including those who work all the time, will pay more. Clearly, the government thinks, as do some members of the opposition including the hon. member who spoke before me, that many drawing unemployment insurance do not want to work and are not trying to find jobs. Many hon. members receive complaints almost daily from constituents who have drawn unemployment insurance and been cut off from benefits because, in the opinion of the benefit control officer, they have not looked energetically enough for
work.	.
Although the commission has intensified its aggressive investigation of people drawing benefits to make sure that benefits are only paid to those with bona fide entitlement, to those looking for and available for work, and although the commission has disqualified and cut off from benefits thousands who had been drawing unemployment insurance, the government obviously believes that many are drawing benefits who ought not to be.
I do not suggest for a moment that there are not people drawing benefits who ought not to be drawing them. I do not suggest that all on unemployment insurance are actively looking for work, as I am sure some are not. But I believe the number in that category is small. The government and some opposition members obviously believe that the number is large. The minister therefore proposes that those who are unlikely ever to be unemployed shall pay a substantially increased weekly premium because a few people are ripping off the system.
Is that not a strange view of the just society? Is it right to ask people who work steadily, who contribute to the fund and who many never draw benefits, to pay larger premiums? The government thinks this is necessary- partly because the government's misguided economic policies have led to the highest levels of unemployment since the beginning of World War II, and partly because it thinks some people are ripping off the system.
Let me voice further objections to the government's proposals. I object strongly to the provision under which people who voluntarily leave their employment will be disqualified from benefit for a certain extra period. According to the minister, about 25,000 people per year voluntarily leave their jobs. That is less than 2.5 per cent

October 29, 1975

of our labour force-hardly an alarming figure to justify so harsh an amendment. We shall never know how much hardship that provision will create, as we shall not know how many workers would quit their jobs but for this amendment. For example, a worker may work in a plant in which the high dust level is a hazard to health. I can tell the minister that during the last three or four years CPR workers have complained to me about unbelievably high dust levels in the repair shops. All their complaints to the federal Department of Labour have been to no avail.
We know-I will not make a long speech about it-about the dangers arising from asbestos dust in Arvida and other towns in Quebec. We know about workers at Elliot Lake who have fallen victim to cancer. If the worker decides that his job is a health hazard and that he must quit, to look for another job, he will be penalized unless he can satisfy some faceless bureaucrat of the Unemployment Insurance Commission that he had a legitimate reason for quitting.
I will not be overly critical of Unemployment Insurance Commission employees. They are trying to do their job, but they are only human; they can make mistakes. I wonder how they will deal with the extra burden of appeals this legislation will impose on them. I, for one, am not prepared to see the kind of decision-making I have spoken of relegated to some commission employee in Winnipeg, Vancouver or Toronto. I do not think the government needs to introduce so draconian an amendment to cover the 2.5 per cent of our labour force who quit their jobs voluntarily. If that particular provision is passed, many workers who have legitimate reason to be dissatisfied or unhappy with their jobs will not be able to quit. Many cannot afford the penalty of forgoing three weeks of unemployment insurance benefit while they look for a job. Therefore, they will stay on a job they do not like, a job to which they are not suited, and there will be adverse effects on health. Frankly, I am amazed that the minister would propose that kind of amendment.
The bill proposes the reduction of benefit rates paid to claimants with dependants. It would reduce the rate from 75 per cent of regular earnings to 66% per cent. The 75 per cent only applied to claimants whose earnings were less than the maximum of $185 per week or less than $62 in benefits. The government's reasoning that family benefit payments have increased since the act came into force is surely not sufficient to justify this amendment.
The area I represent is not particularly low wage in character. Therefore, I cannot speak with the same personal knowledge and experience as the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) who spoke earlier today. However, this Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who talked so eloquently and frequently in earlier times about his concept of a just society, and this government should not be bringing in amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act which will have the effect of cutting back drastically the benefits of those who need them most in order to meet the most minimal living expenses.
I want to register my opposition to the amendment which terminates unemployment insurance coverage for those 65 years old and defers Canada Pension Plan ben-
Unemployment Insurance Act
efits during the permissible three-week lump sum termination payment. Improved federal and provincial income support programs for workers aged 65 and over should not be an excuse for depriving them of their unemployment insurance benefits. This amendment hits hardest those with low incomes who are not covered by a private pension plan and whose payments under the Canada Pension Plan are inadequate. Those who for economic or other reasons must continue work after age 65 will not be able to draw unemployment insurance benefits, as has been the case in the past.
In my years as a member of parliament I have been approached by dozens of people who have paid unemployment insurance premiums since the day the plan began in 1940 and were never unemployed and never received a penny in unemployment insurance benefits. I have heard the argument that this is an insurance plan and they are lucky if they have never been unemployed and have not received any benefits. If one is dealing solely with statistics, that is a good argument. However, we are not dealing with statistics; we are dealing with people who have contributed to the plan for 30 or more years and are entitled to some benefits.
We live in an age where it is believed that a person aged 65, 67 or 63 should be required to retire on a fixed day because it is better for both the individual and the company. However, we are beginning to realize that if it ever was a good idea, it is no longer. People should have the option of retiring from active work when they feel it is good for them and their employer. I do not mean that a person should be able to retire at age 35 or 40, but we should be aiming for a situation where a person can choose when to retire from age 60 on.
If we believe that some people should retire at age 60, and it is better for others to work until they are 66, 67 or 69, we should make our system as flexible as possible. People ought not to be told that if they work past age 65 they will not be entitled to receive the benefits of the unemployment insurance plan to which they contributed for so many years.
I began my speech by pointing out how different the approach of this minister was in introducing this bill from the approach of the former minister of manpower when introducing the bill dealing with unemployment insurance benefits in 1971. The former minister was hopeful, optimistic and cheerful. We went along with him. We did not think the 1971 bill was perfect, that it was another commandment which would last for all time; however, we thought it was a good move in the right direction. We had some criticisms and we made some suggestions for improvements, some of which were accepted and many of which were rejected. On the whole, the bill was an improvement and we supported it.
If there are any improvements in this bill, they are almost accidental. On the whole, it is a disaster from the first word to the last. The four provisions which I have outlined are bad. There are others that I have not dealt with which are equally bad. These will be dealt with by other members of the New Democratic Party. The bill in its present form leaves us no alternative but to oppose it on second reading. We will try to amend it in committee.
October 29, 1975

Unemployment Insurance Act
Unless there is a substantial change of heart on the part of the government, we will oppose it on third reading.
What the minister is saying is that the government, having promoted measures which, as was predicted by many both inside and outside the House, have increased the rate of unemployment to the highest it has been in 15 years and the second highest since 1940, now expects the people of Canada to pay for its mistakes by higher taxes in the form of higher contributions by employers and employees to the unemployment insurance fund. We cannot support such a proposal and we will oppose it as much as we can.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank you for allowing me to rise at this time in the debate on second reading of the bill to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act of 1971. I was really anxious to speak on this bill because of the personal experiences of my fellow citizens in the riding I have the honour of representing who may have had problems with the Unemployment Insurance Commission since 1971.
First of all, I want to say to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras), who is now present in the House that all is not rotten with the commission, and that it is with a positive attitude that I want to approach the bill now before the House.
Madam Speaker, I should like to synthesize my remarks, though I may come back to some at a later stage in the processing of the bill. I should first of all stress the fact, to the minister, that there is much criticism, much abuse, not in the act itself but in its practical application where benefits are concerned. This in turn involves human relations, within the system of structures of the unemployment insurance offices, between the employee who receives the claims and the claimant.
Everyone will admit with me that this legislation is very complicated. Its characteristic before being satisfactory is to be complicated. It is so complicated that the employees of various unemployment insurance offices do not agree on its interpretation and most of the problems experienced by my own claimants are specifically due to the fact that communications between a given unemployment insurance office and the claimant are difficult and generally badly organized. And then the Unemployment Insurance Act has never been popularized-or simplified in every day words that the claimant can understand. I will give you only one example to show how the legislation is complicated.
I have seen a number of cases, Madam Speaker, where a mother on the labour market was advised by her physician to quit work because she was pregnant. However this woman cannot draw any benefit because she is in the re-established portion of her benefit period. That is why she cannot draw unemployment insurance benefits throughout her pregnancy.
Now what is that re-establishment period? Madam Speaker, I have taken a count during four months and the figures were checked by the local Drummondville office. The figures which I will quote are accurate. I received at my Victoriaville office 1095 complaints concerning unem-

ployment insurance, that is only for half of my constituency. And of those 1095 complaints referred to the minister, most were the victims of a misunderstanding or a wrong interpretation of the legislation.
In either case, Madam Speaker, I do not care who is at fault. The important thing to note at this point in the debate is that it is always best for legislators to simplify, give a thorough explanation of measures passed if they are to achieve their purpose.
Madam Speaker, the first problem that cannot escape my notice is the centralization of payments. I know very well that the matter is not included in amendments to the act before us and it is unfortunate. It concerns the internal organization of the commission and is related so closely to the effectiveness of the implementation of the legislation introduced by the minister that I cannot help bringing it up.
Such a centralized payment system has been established that each province has only one distributing office. In the province of Quebec, for instance, the only office authorized to pay benefits to any unemployed person is located in Montreal.
If a problem arises, for example delays in the payment of benefits, an error in the punched cards which makes the computer in Montreal unable to digest them, it will result in the claimant having to wait for two, three, four, five, eight and sometimes ten weeks or more before getting his first cheque.
Madam Speaker, I think this is now the main problem with the Unemployment Insurance Commission. The delays regarding payments. Let us forget for a moment the two-week waiting period in the case of ordinary unemployment or the three-week waiting period, according to the former legislation, in the case of a worker who has voluntarily quit his job. This period would be doubled under the amendments now proposed. It remains, Madam Speaker, that given our experience of this legislation since 1971, because of this bad centralization, the average claimant will have to suffer a two-week waiting period. He will get paid only at the end of the fourth week or after a four-week unemployment period. Now, the computer in Montreal, the payment centre for the whole province, does not issue cheques at the end of the fourth week. This will take in general one or two weeks, in addition to the waiting period and to the two weeks of unemployment before the person receives the first benefit cheque.
It then no longer is a good organization. This has terrible consequences on the situation of the family, on the income of the family and the worker. Not all Canadian workers can afford to wait for six or seven weeks before they receive the first benefits.
The main problem is that these payments are unduly delayed because of centralization. Madam Speaker, I take advantage of the minister's presence to bring this problem to his attention. I wish the commission would revise its position in that respect and accept to divide the province of Quebec into two or three payment regions, in order to speed up things.
At the present time, we unfortunately have a postal strike. We can imagine the vast organization the department has had to set up in Montreal to deliver benefits
October 29, 1975

across Quebec. It is absolutely unbelievable what efforts have to be made to reach an unemployed in Baie-Comeau, Sainte-Croix of Lotbiniere, Chicoutimi, Sherbrooke, or Sainte-Marie of Beauce, by bus or otherwise, and see to it that he gets his unemployment insurance.
When there is a strike, the minister has to set up emergency offices here and there throughout the province because of the communications problem. I want to say to the minister that even when the situation is normal, when there is no strike, undue delays are still blamed on this payment centre.
Doubtless several hon. members know that it takes only one claimant's card to block the whole system in the province of Quebec.
Madam Speaker, the day the problem will be dealt with, there will be a delay of two to three weeks to recover the punched card of the claimant and to pay him. So, when we communicate with them they answer: give us two weeks to be able to issue the first allowance cheque. Then the machine is so peeved by the intervention of a third party that it churns out order payments for 3,4,5,8, or 10 cheques, supposedly for the arrears for the claimant which very often do not correspond to the real weeks of unemployment.
Thus, there is overpayment. Hence, Madam Speaker, there is a second problem stemming from the centralization of payments, namely that overpayments-and I am anxious to see the statistical analysis of the minister in this regard-are generally due to the fact that two or three extra weeks are paid with the arrears. So, later not only will this man have to wait for two or even three weeks when he is again unemployed. He will also have to make without the allowances for 2,3 or 4 weeks, namely the equivalent of the overpayment received during the previous period of unemployment.
One may say it is very complicated. Yet it is very simple. All that need be done, technically, is to divide in a logical way the present regional unemployment insurance offices into decentralized pay centres, regionalized for the whole province. Thus, delays could be prevented.
It must be remembered that this legislation covers workers with lower income in general and that when they are on unemployment for the first waiting weeks that is a two-week waiting period and two weeks payable at the end, they use up their savings if they happen to have some. Unemployment is a dramatic situation for a family. Those unemployed must not be the victims of a machine which decides who gets what. Concluding on this first point, I urge the minister to accept at least investigation, a study on the speed at which payments are made, on the profitability and efficiency of the centralized system in operation since 1971. This would be a definite improvement which will be reflected in the opinion people have of the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
I would say that 80 per cent of the criticisms directed at the commission involve delays in receiving benefits. The remaining 20 per cent is due to either the overcomplexity or the underpopularization of the act. But, if the former shortcomings, involving 80 per cent of the complaints,
Unemployment Insurance Act
could be corrected, Madam Speaker, I am sure many hon. members of this House, at any rate those from Quebec would be very pleased to have that much less office work. I have experienced that I can receive as many as 25 or 30 calls in a single day in my office in Victoriaville, and upon examination of the complaints I invariably realize they concern overdue benefits. All this because of the Montreal computer.
Madam Speaker, the other problem that I wanted to bring forward from the beginning concerns civil servants. There are some unemployment insurance officers-I suppose in every local office has a few-who assume a haughty and domineering attitude in their dealings with the applicants. I wish to congratulate the minister for accepting to alter the inquiry procedure. It is a well known fact that, until now, a claim officer had the authority to call unexpectedly on an applicant and simply start the process of investigation. We all know how easy it is to have somebody tell anything to anyone, it all depends on the way to put the question. Consequently, some people, by their statements during a friendly discussion with the officer, would virtually hang themselves just because they were being too friendly with the person taking the statement.
The minister recently said that this method would be abolished, that the individual making the statement would be entitled to have a witness and that he will not have to sign the statement as it could turn against him later because he ignores the law.
Madam Speaker, I think that, at that time the minister was courageous, that he actually broke this system of provocation, of police and inquests and that, on that point, he deserves congratulations. Let us hope that the system will work well.
The third point that I wanted to make concerns illness. Madam Speaker, I believe that there are three possibilities: ordinary unemployment, unemployment because of pregnancy and unemployment because of illness. For my part, I believe that the most dramatic and the most serious type of unemployment is the one which occurs when the claimant loses or quits his job because of illness.
In that case, Madam Speaker, even the new legislation introduced today by the minister changes practically nothing in the situation except to extend the admissibility period from 29 to 39 weeks. But the problem is that the UIC officer always has authority to determine the length of the claimant's illness. The officer, who is not a physician, is given this authority in the present legislation, and I am sorry that the minister is not amending this provision. The officer, and the physician designated by the commission have the authority to determine the length of the illness, regardless of the report of the claimant's personal physician.
Madam Speaker, I believe that we should have some confidence in the physicians and their professional ethics. When the claimant has a liver attack on the job and his physician states that he is unable to work and that he must be hospitalised to have an operation and tells him that he will have to remain at home in convalescence during a fixed period, such as 20 weeks, the commission has the authority after two, three, five, seven or ten weeks, in spite of the report of the claimant's personal physician,

October 29, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
to say that claims are not paid for more than eight, ten or twelve weeks in the case of liver trouble.
It is completely ridiculous to have given such excessive discretionary powers to the officer to allow him to determine the length of an illness when the person involved is unable to defend himself. He is sick and cannot go to the regional office to state his case to the officer. He cannot complete a statement since he is in hospital or on the operating table, and it is precisely this part of the legislation which is the most rigorous. There is no leniency in a case of illness at the UIC.
People who have a heart attack are entitled to be sick for 15 weeks, people who have a liver attack are entitled to so many weeks, those who have the flu are entitled to so many weeks, regardless of the fact that it is broncho-pneumonia, or that the flu was followed by laryngitis or that there were other sequelae.
The official does not care about that. Neither does the act. Under the act, if you have a slight cough, you are entitled to two weeks, whether or not your sore throat turns into a lung disease or if you lose one or both lungs.
Madam Speaker, this is a ridiculous situation. And when the claimant wants to speak in his own defence and appeals to the arbitration board to try and get more, supposing of course he is physically able to appear in court, the doctor in attendance very seldom has time to go and explain himself his decision.
Let me also add, Madam Speaker, that generally, doctors appointed by the Commission to complete a medical certificate in the name of the Commission very frequently do so, and I know this is very serious, without even examining the patient, without having ever seen him. How can the doctor appointed by the Commission, who has never seen the claimant, who does not sound his chest either, who examines him only superficially, say that a person will need a two, three or five week convalescence?
Madam Speaker, such situations occur every day in Lotbiniere, in Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean, in the Beauce area, and throughout the country. I know from numerous cases that it is a human problem that people find revolting and which I submit to the minister through you, Madam Speaker. As I said earlier, claimants who are ill are not in a position where they can take their own defence by the very reason of their illness.
Madam Speaker, the minister has taken a small step forward by extending the qualifying period in the case of illness from 29 to 39 weeks. However, this is almost meaningless. In the past, an individual who received standard unemployment benefits and who after weeks had a relapse and was unemployed, was entitled to benefits for that incomplete qualifying period.
The minister has taken a very small and not very courageous step by extending that period to 39 weeks and thus, Madam Speaker, it will still be possible in that case, in spite of that supposedly tremendous legislation, to find pregnant women who are unable to work on the advice of their physician and who having received standard unemployment benefits for one, two, three or five weeks will be denied any before their confinement, because the qualify-

ing period is not long enough and because the condition of that individual will not have been taken into consideration.
Madam Speaker, there are only two answers: either we encourage birth either we encourage abortion. And if the minister does not change that part of the legislation concerning pregnancy I think it will encourage abortion as, in most cases, pregnant women who received benefits during winter cannot receive them anymore.
I believe and I sincerely hope that the minister will entirely revise the part of the legislation concerning sickness and that during each stage of the debate and particularly the committee stage we will try to improve that part of the legislation. Thus we respect sick people, we help them when they most need help and, in case of pregnancy, we stop pussyfooting around and say once for all that we believe in the family and encourage mothers to have their child by paying them their 15 weeks of unemployment benefits for the period of confinement without bothering them and taking into account the other periods in the 104-week qualifying period mentioned by the minister in the bill.
I do not wish to say anything more on the subject. I think I clearly expressed what I had to say to the minister and I sincerely hope he will take it into account.
The third point that troubles me before I come to the positive aspects of the legislation in pension at 65. Through this act, the minister unacknowledgedly imposes pension at 65. He does it in the way retirement was imposed at 70. He does not say so, of course, as it would be unpopular. But when you deprive workers 65 years old or more from all their rights under the pretext that they receive retirement benefits plus a supplement, the minister misleads us and does not take the actual situation into account. He says that does not affect many people. I got in touch with Statistics Canada in that respect; I wanted to know just how many workers between the ages of 65 and 69 were still on the labour market. And the answer is 619,940 workers between the ages of 65 and 69, a figure I got yesterday afternoon from Statistics Canada. Between 65 and 70, in all that is including everyone up to 75, 1,124,000 workers will be in that situation, meaning they will lose entirely their rights to unemployment insurance although they worked for 25, 30, 40 and 50 years and conformed to all government legislation, good or bad, during all their lives.
Madam Speaker, the minister is too intelligent not to be aware of the consequences of his legislation and not to have foreseen them. In short, he imposes mandatory retirement at 65. He says under the same legislation, if you want to continue to work, you are free to do so, but do not count on us to protect you. As far as we are concerned, you no longer have any rights, you are a worker and you are such a nuisance to us, we want you out of the labour market so much that we are taking your rights away from you. That is the situation in which we are going to place people aged 65 or more.
The minister simply wants to push out of the labour market anyone aged 65 or more. When he introduced his bill on second reading, the minister said this was because those people received OAS and guaranteed income supplement increases. As I understand OAS schedules, a worker
October 29, 1975

is not entitled to the supplement because of his earnings. He generally gets the maximum amount of pension and a few dollars of supplement. Therefore, the minister's suggestion that a person in the labour force can get a pension over $200 is misleading. The Quebec offices of the official, Mr. Gerard Turbide, can confirm that. The supplement is granted according to revenues. The basic pension is paid equally to every citizen. The minister wants to persuade workers over 65 to retire, because OAS pensions are based not on the current year's revenues but on those of the previous year. This tends to show how unfair the minister's proposal is. The income supplement given a worker in 1975 is based on his 1974 revenues. Assuming a worker aged 65 retired on January 1, 1976, he would be without revenues other than the basic old age security pension. He would then get a supplement application form in which he would have to declare his 1974 revenues. Therefore, he would not be entitled to supplement for that year as of 1976, so long as a new computation was not made. Such is the current situation. I hear some members opposite say this is not true. Well, I will not debate this. Tomorrow, I shall try to meet them and show them examples I have of this. It would be astounding if they wished to remedy this, because it is schedules.

speechtext: That is optional.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
That may be optional, however, that is compulsory retirement. I wonder if the minister checked in the labour market to get employers' opinion. A number of employers will regret that. People of 65 who still want to work and still have the courage to do so are generally excellent workers who give great satisfaction to their employers. This is a recognized fact. Most of them work not for the fun of it, but only because they have insufficient means.
Madam Speaker, I hope that the minister will take it upon himself to withdraw completely this proposal and leave things as they are. We should respect the worker who has worked all his life and leave the age at 70. Of course, if the minister does not want to do it himself, I shall be forced to oppose the bill completely in view of the enormous social repercussions that it will have on those who are 65.
As the previous speaker said, we have been using ringing phrases like "just society". Can a single member of the government tell me that it is just, after 50 or 40 years of work, to take away all the rights of a worker only because to his age even if he still wants to work for the good of his country? If they can justify this bill from the point of view of justice and fairness, Madam Speaker, I shall have to accept it since they have the majority, and this would be regrettable. But I do not believe that the government members can defend this bill.
The last point I wanted to make is as follows: in 1974, at least 265,831 workers were penalized for having voluntarily quit their job. In the legislation proposed by the minister, the waiting period is doubled, which means that any one quitting his job will, in principle, have to wait eight weeks before receiving his first cheque. Madam Speaker, I have myself very often been before the arbitration board with my fellow citizens to defend their rights.
Unemployment Insurance Act
In almost 99.9 per cent of all cases where my people were accused of quitting voluntarily, we won our case and the commission ruled in our favour. But in all cases, never did an employer come himself to give his own version. Two weeks ago, I went before the board of referees in Drummondville. A certain employer maintained that a young lady had quit her job in a beauty parlor. That employer had sent a letter to downgrade completely the young hairdresser. When we showed up before the board of referees, there were the members of the board, the claimant, the secretary of the board and myself. The employer was not there. Even though he had condemned the young lady and had put her in a defensive position before the board, under an unduly complicated law, that man was absent. He had not even been invited or summoned. To have his revenge because he was losing a good employee and I suppose because he had not accepted the wage demands of the employee-another possible reason- the employer had written a letter which was against the interest of a young lady who had worked for him for three years.
In any case, Madam Speaker, that proves that if the minister really wants to have a truly effective legislation, which will prompt workers to keep their job, he must give claimants better protection against those who could abuse.
If we are going to adopt that part of the legislation against which I have nothing in principle, it remains that employers now wield an extraordinary weapon. They will be able to provoke their employees particularly where there is no union and we know that in my riding in Quebec many workers are not organized. Employers will be able to provoke their employees for any kind of reason knowing full well that no employee will dare quit his job lest he lose his income for eight weeks. And as the claimant has the onus of proving that he did not leave his job voluntarily and without cause, inevitably any fault is considered his but never the employer's.
I deplore, I must admit, such coercive measures which are very harsh and in which the employer has no role to play. When an employee is hired there are always two persons involved, he and the employer. When people work in factories, there are always two groups, the employers and the employees. But when somebody is laid off, the decision rests on one, the employer while the employee depends on this decision.
If an employee leaves his job, here again we find two parties-the employer and the employee. Who decided the employee should leave? To be fair in applying such a rigorous legislation, one should instruct each employer that every time an employee voluntarily leaves his job he should produce his version of the facts and even appear before the board of referees and justify the reasons why the employee left and why he was put by the employer in a situation where he was forced to leave his job.
With this eight-week system, we are going to see a number of abuses, particularly among the workers, if we fail to give them the protection they require. Madam Speaker, I was reading, I cannot remember exactly where, that last year 144,000 unemployment insurance claimants had been declared ineligible by the CMC because they had
8682

October 29, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
not looked for a job, a decision which was taken on the strength of a single report. A number of members of this House have certainly heard of similar cases. After a certain unemployment period, the Commission communicates with the CMC officers and ask them to look for a job to propose one to the unemployed or to check if the claimants are actually looking for one.
One unilateral report from an anonymous manpower centre is enough to disentitle a claimant. All of a sudden the claimant sees himself deprived of all his rights. And the appeal procedure starts all over again. When the claimant appears before the board of referees to prove he made efforts to find a job, the manpower centre does not attend the board of referees' hearing either.
Madam Speaker, everything is set in a complex legislation so that the claimant is always the one who has the onus of proving his innocence, so to speak. In the board of referees procedure mentioned in the legislation, the minister will have to add provisions about employers who make all kinds of reports. I learned that in 1974, as many as 32,382 workers lost their jobs on account of misconduct. Alcohol or the irresponsibility of the employee may be the causes of misconduct, but it could also be due to an employer who exploits his employee. And yet, I think that there is not even 2 per cent of those cases of misconduct where the employer is required to give evidence before the board of referees.
Thus the claimant, and only the claimant, has to face the three members of the board of referees and has to put up his own defence against the Unemployment Insurance Commission, its act and regulations, and God knows how involved some of them are, and against an employer who has charged him with misconduct when he entered the word "misconduct" on his separation certificate. The employer is merely required to put down his firm name, the number of weeks worked and the word "misconduct". That is the employer's sole obligation. This means that any employer could put down the word "misconduct" on any employee's separation certificate and thus create a social tragedy, a human tragedy for a claimant when actually there may have been no misconduct at all. There again, the claimant has the onus of proving it while there is none for the employer.	_
I think that this is one of the act's serious shortcomings. I will conclude my remarks on this, Madam Speaker. I would still have many more to make, but I will limit myself to these on second reading, and I will perhaps hark back to it before the committee, at the report and third reading stages. I would like to summarize and say that the part dealing with 65 is-year-olds is, to us, absolutely inacceptable, unfair, and is even provocative for workers of 65 or over. It does not recognize their rights. It systematically withdraws them.
Madam Speaker, the second point is the decentralization of unemployment insurance benefit payments. I think that the minister cannot justify, defend or continue to defend such centralization in payments. The third point is the review process, that is the appeal process provided in the act. Provisions should be added so that employers and manpower centres that make reports on workers be also required by law to give their own views on the facts to ensure that the act is not a cause of inequity but a source of satisfaction and justice for workers.

I think the appeal procedure, the arbitration at the board of referees or before an umpire is an important means of checking whether there has been an error of judgment. As far as I know, before any court, there are always two parties. I think that before the board of referees, which is not a court but a place where people try to understand each other as well as possible, there should be as many statements of facts as possible.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, those of my colleagues who preceded me this afternoon in the debate on Bill C-69 pointed out, some of them with great eloquence I felt, the weaknesses in present operation of UIC offices. They also highlighted, rather spectacularly, I thought, and here I am thinking of the hon. members for St. John East (Mr. McGrath) and Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin), the effects some of the provisions of the bill will have, in their opinion, on Canadians.
I should like to take the next few minutes to introduce also into this debate a note which, I think, will make the statements more consistent with everyday occurrences in Canada. Before doing so, I wish to remind you, Madam Speaker, that the unemployment insurance plan has been in effect for 35 years in Canada.
Canada did not break new ground in the field of unemployment insurance. Several European countries have had unemployment insurance for more than five centuries. Several even brought it in early in the 20th century. In Canada, the legislator became conscious of his role and of his responsibility to adopt income support measures only after the great economic depression of the thirties.
The first legislation on investments and social insurance passed in 1935 gave rise to many debates and even to conflicts of jurisdiction. As a matter of fact, some provinces had questioned the authority of the federal government to legislate in the field of unemployment insurance. A decision of the judicial committee of the Privy Council was required to define whether the Canadian government had full jurisdiction in the field of insurance.
But this legislation of 1935, the Investment and Social Insurance Act, was an act which sanctioned inequality to some extent. First, inequality concerning the age and also concerning facts. For instance, a young woman aged 16 or 17 could not receive weekly benefits exceeding $1.50 while a man 21 or over could receive more than $6 a week. Those figures, Madam Speaker, may seem a little ridiculous in the context of today's income scale, but they do shed light on the evolution of mentalities, priorities and, mostly, responsibilities of the Canadian government. No need to recall that current weekly benefits can amount to $123 and that they are based in the insurable income of the claimant during the qualifying period.
Madam Speaker, the role of unemployment insurance in Canada, is essential to maintain a certain economic stability. There are many factors in favour of maintaining unemployment insurance. One only has to bear in mind that the level of relative wealth in the various regions of Canada varies throughout the country, that social, geographical and even climatic conditions play a prominent part in the income scale of Canadians.
October 29, 1975

Madam Speaker, it is interesting to bear in mind that over 2.1 per cent of the gross national product in Canada is made up of unemployment insurance benefits. You will agree with me to what extent unemployment insurance benefits have a stabilizing effect on the income level and growth of the Canadian people in the Maritimes, in the North, in all areas of this country with different climatic conditions from one season to another.
Indeed, Madam Speaker, it must be known and kept in mind that unemployment benefits are not intended only as income support for claimants, they are also designed to maintain a decent income level within a community, to maintain, for example, within a particular community the level of public expenditures, the level of consumer expenditures, the level of rents, the level of owner expenditures at an acceptable rate.
And that is why, Madam Speaker, in the present situation, even with an excessively high rate of unemployment exceeding 7 per cent, and my colleagues referred to it this afternoon, that is why, Madam Speaker, in countries as important as the United States where there are more than eight million jobless, that is why also in countries like Japan, western countries like Great Britain, France, where the total number of unemployed now exceeds 14 million, in those countries there is no social unrest similar to that we experienced during the thirties or even similar to that Germany experienced, for example, during the twenties.
Unemployment benefits and unemployment insurance indeed play a significant stabilizing part in every industrialised nation, a stabilizing part which affects not only the economy but social life as well. And I believe that in discussing amendments to unemployment insurance it is essential to bear in mind their possible impact on the social atmosphere.
Of course, Madam Speaker, the plan in force since 1935 has been extensively overhauled. The law enacted in 1971, in particular, provided for automatic and annual equalization between premium rates and amounts of insurable earnings. Each year, therefore, the amount of insurable earnings of each Canadian worker and the premium he must contribute to the plan and to the unemployment insurance account are continually readjusted.
Madam Speaker, looking at those amendments which are before us today, I think we should be pleased to see that to a certain extent the minister and the government are conscious of their responsibility in continuously improving the unemployment insurance scheme. And before I comment on some of the proposed amendments which raise more questions than others, I think it is essential that I should repeat that at least three of them tend to achieve a balance which will prove beneficial to the entire system.
The first of these wise and desirable amendments, in my opinion, concerns the payment of travelling expenses incurred by a claimant or his representative when they have to appear before the board of referees. My honorable colleagues have mentioned and shown most convincingly how difficult it is in many instances for a worker to appear before a board of referees. If, on top of having to prove his case, the claimant has to pay for expenses incurred by his representative, I think there is an anomaly which should be corrected. As a matter of fact, in civil as well as criminal cases, somte of the expenses of the parties
Unemployment Insurance Act
who manage to prove their case are assumed by the court and by the departments of Justice.
Madam Speaker, I think in this instance, it is quite logical for the Unemployment Insurance Commission to pay for the expenses of the claimant or his representative, whether he be a lawyer, a union representative or even a member of parliament as in the case of the hon. member for Lotbiniere. And I think it should be stressed that this amendment brings into the system an element of fairness which we all welcome.
The second amendment which, in our opinion, also relates to the desire for a balanced income, is the one which deals with qualification for benefits for a supplementary period of 104 weeks. Many Canadian workers find themselves in situations which disqualify or would disqualify them because they cannot complete that 104-week period. For instance, someone who must serve a jail sentence, who is temporarily disabled or who for various reasons, sickness or quarantine, must stay away from his job. I think that the amendment designed to complete that 104-week period restores the balance and the justice we wish to see in the system.
There are also more specific details in the definition of some terms that will also restore the balance. For instance, the definition and the details of the expression "suitable employment", the extension of benefit period in case of sickness and the authorization for the claimant to withdraw a claim will certainly contribute to restore that basic justice, the natural justice that was lacking during the trial periods of the system since 1971. Obviously, we have not heard the last of it and all the reforms needed are not contained in Bill C-69. It is easy to see for instance that one of the main defects which is not corrected in the bill concerns the consolidation of arbitration awards.
Having completed law studies, you know as well as I do, Madam Speaker, that one of the judicial guarantees is the knowledge by law officers of decisions rendered by the courts in earlier cases. It is important that workers and insured persons may eventually have access to an office consolidation of arbitration awards. I believe this would bring some uniformity into the plan, because it is realized that counsel, judges and arbitrators may have a different perception, different practices and various degrees of knowledge of the law from one area to the other. I believe it is important to standardize the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I will not insist on the complexity of the act. Every member in this House knows how many interpretation "unexpectabilities" must be faced when advising a voter or a citizen that consults us on the act. I believe the first guarantee we should seek to add to this legislation is precisely that of an administrative consolidation of arbitration awards, or at least a data centre on decisions awarded on the most stupid points, the most questioned ones or those that give rise to the largest number of problems with the insured.
A second amendment that should be introduced involves the number of days during which an employee, a worker has not worked at his job but may have returned to some part-time employment. It is realized that these periods of
29669-66%

October 29, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
disqualification, these loss of benefit periods very often induce claimants not to apply for employment or make any effort to accept temporary work. I believe the regulations should be reviewed at that level. This would bring some measure of justice that would better account for the desire of Canadians to work, as evidenced by the extra 104-week period applying to Canadian workers who had to momentarily leave the labour market.
Madam Speaker, this legislation aimed at giving the Unemployment Insurance Commission some credibility in the eyes of the Canadian people was not the only one passed since 1971. Previous speakers in this debate have shown to what extent the government's estimates of unemployment insurance administration costs have been wrong or low during the years which followed the amendment of the plan in 1971. I refer my colleagues to the estimates for 1973-74 where they will find that there was only a difference of 0.3 per cent between the costs anticipated in 1972 and the costs incurred in 1973. I believe, Madam Speaker, that in the case of a plan as complex as unemployment insurance, there is now some misunderstanding and a certain administration control which can lead us to think that we are on the right track.
Moreover, Madam Speaker, especially in 1972, bitter criticism has been heaped on the workers about the rip-off artists, about the people who collected benefits without trying hard enough to find employment. An article published in the Globe and Mail in April 1975 reported that more than 50,000 claimants would be prosecuted or have to return money within the next months. Madam Speaker, I think that if Canadians are to maintain their confidence in the system, not only must they be assured that justice is done within the system but also that justice appears to be done. In that sense, Madam Speaker, there is also room for important amendments. My colleagues have noted how employers seldom appear before boards of referees and how very little they have to do with the application procedures of the system.
I would like to say, Madam Speaker, that many employers fail or refuse to send their employment statement formula in the time prescribed under the program. If the program must be tightened, or if it must show fairness to those who do get undeserved benefits, I think it must also be severe and just as inflexible against those employers who do not comply with conditions and provisions of the law.
In my opinion, Madam Speaker, if this system is to be balanced, this also applies to employers, and I am sure that the amendments under consideration will not remain a dead letter in the minister's ear.
In fact, the minister has showed such availability and openmindedness in recent years that we are sympathetic to any amendment that could be proposed in this system.
Of course Bill C-69 still features three amendments that give rise to questions. These amendments, Madam Speaker, concern the disqualification of people aged 65. I do not support my colleagues's opinion that disqualifying people who reach age 65 deprives them of the right to work.
True, Madam Speaker, such disqualification prevents them from getting unemployment insurance benefits. In my opinion, Madam Speaker, if we want to have a true
(Mr. Joyal.]
picture of the situation, we must pay more heed to the statistics referred to by my colleague. Madam Speaker, I am eager to acquaint you with Statistics Canada figures concerning people over 65. The persons who took part in the survey conducted by Statistics Canada stated unanimously that there are fewer workers who report as unemployed than there are claimants.
This seems to indicate that those people tell the investigators that they are not seeking employment and are not interested in working, while at the same time collecting benefits and telling the Commission they are actively looking for a job.
Therefore, it is becoming more and more difficult from an administrative point of view to ascertain whether or not unemployed over 65 really wish to find a job. The situation is as follows, Madam Speaker. In Quebec, for instance, some 16,000 claimants aged 65 or over now get unemployment insurance benefits. According to a survey made by Statistics Canada, about 8,000 of them, that is 50 per cent are in fact looking for work, and are actually interested in getting a job.
Consequently, we have this imbalance in the very objectives of the program which, of course, are to support income while also encouraging the unemployed to seek out work, and the will of the claimants who have reached the age of 65 to look for work and get a job.
The bill as proposed by the minister is a drastic one. It automatically excludes all persons who have reached the age of 65 and who get a pension from either the Canada Pension Plan or the Quebec Pension Plan. Madam Speaker, I think there is a happy medium which would probably allow us to solve the problem where the average claimant, of over 65 wants to withdraw from the working force while, on the other hand, wanting to get the maximum benefits to which he is entitled; and considering current contributions, that could amount to $6,373. I believe there must be a middle course to answer the purpose of the system. The bill, as proposed by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, provides that any worker who is 65 and receives the pension benefits be given compensation equivalent to three weeks' unemployment insurance benefits.
I believe, Madam Speaker, that a worker who is 65 should be able to choose whether he wants to receive at 65 these three weeks of benefits proposed in the bill of the minister or to carry on within the system. In that latter case, he should be subject to all the controls and conditions of the bill. It has been found out, Madam Speaker, under the administration in recent months, that since 1971 half the claimants were not actually looking for jobs but that the commission officials, responsible for controls and investigation, hesitated to sue a 66-year-old employee because he had not taken the trouble to fill the necessary forms or to actually look for a job. Obviously, to harass someone who is 68 years old and who depends for his living on the unemployment insurance payments seems particularly odious and unbearable. But Madam Speaker, I believe that in this situation, there must be a middle course to be found and I believe it should be considered if we want this legislation to pass bringing more equity, the necessary support and incentives to work. I believe, Madam Speaker, that it is 6 o'clock.
October 29, 1975
